Great question — and very relevant to genealogy research, since Quaker records are among the most detailed and well-preserved in colonial and early American history, but their dating conventions trip up many researchers.

## Why Quakers Used Numbered Months

### The Religious Reason

The Society of Friends (Quakers), founded by George Fox in England in the 1650s, were deeply committed to stripping away anything they considered worldly corruption or idolatry — including **pagan names embedded in the calendar**.

The problem was that both month and weekday names honored pagan gods:

| Name | Pagan Origin |
|---|---|
| January | *Janus*, Roman god of beginnings |
| February | *Februa*, Roman purification festival |
| March | *Mars*, Roman god of war |
| May | *Maia*, Roman goddess |
| June | *Juno*, Roman goddess |
| Sunday | the Sun (a deity) |
| Monday | the Moon (a deity) |
| Tuesday | *Tiw*, Norse god |
| Wednesday | *Woden*, Norse god |
| Thursday | *Thor*, Norse god |
| Friday | *Frigg/Freya*, Norse goddess |
| Saturday | *Saturn*, Roman god |

For Quakers, using these names — even casually — felt like giving honor to false gods, which violated their testimonies of truth and simplicity. So they substituted plain numbers: **First Month, Second Month, Third Day, Fifth Day**, etc.

---

## The Critical Genealogical Complication: The Calendar Change of 1752

This is where researchers can make serious errors.

**Before 1752** in England and its colonies, the legal new year began on **March 25** (Lady Day), not January 1. So in Quaker records *before* September 1752:

| Quaker "Month" | Actual Month |
|---|---|
| 1st Month | **March** |
| 2nd Month | April |
| 3rd Month | May |
| ... | ... |
| 10th Month | December |
| 11th Month | January |
| 12th Month | February |

**After 1752**, when Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar and moved New Year's to January 1:

| Quaker "Month" | Actual Month |
|---|---|
| 1st Month | **January** |
| 2nd Month | February |
| 3rd Month | March |
| ... | ... |

So a Quaker record reading **"12th of 3rd Month 1745"** means **May 12, 1745** — *not* March 12th.

---

## Practical Tips for Quaker Records

- **Always check the year** — if it's before 1752, remember the offset
- The transition year 1752 is tricky; records from that year can go either way
- Many Quaker meetings recorded **double dates** during the transition period (e.g., "1st Month / January")
- Meeting minutes, birth records, death records, and marriage certificates all follow this system consistently
- Monthly Meeting records are extremely reliable because Quakers were meticulous record-keepers — making them a genealogical goldmine once you crack the dating system

Would you like help converting specific Quaker dates, or are you working with records from a particular meeting or time period?

Scotland, 1730. Two potential corrections to assess:

| Correction | Applies? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **OS/NS year** (`osNsYear`) | **No** | Scotland changed its year-start from 25 March → 1 January in **1600**, by the Scottish Calendar Act. By 1730, Scotland had used a January 1 year-start for 130 years. No year adjustment is needed. |
| **Julian → Gregorian day** (`julianToGregorianDay`) | **Yes** | Great Britain (including Scotland) did not adopt the Gregorian day reckoning until **September 1752**. In 1730, Scotland was still on the Julian calendar. |

| | Date |

| **Year changed?** | No — year stays 1730 |

### Was the 1752 year-start change relevant for Scotland?

**No — and this is an important point for Scottish research.**

The famous 1752 change (the British Calendar (New Style) Act 1750) bundled two reforms for England, Wales, and Ireland:
1. Move the **legal year-start** from 25 March to 1 January
2. Switch from the **Julian to Gregorian** day reckoning (dropping 11 days)

For **Scotland**, only reform #2 was new in 1752. Reform #1 had already happened in **1600**. So when you encounter a Scottish register entry dated "14 February 1730," the year *14 February* falls in is unambiguous — it is 1730 by both Scottish Old Style and modern reckoning. There is no "1729/30" double-dating ambiguity you'd see in an English record of the same date.

> **Practical tip:** For Scottish records dated **before 1600**, you would need the OS/NS year correction for January–March dates, just as you would for English records before 1752. After 1600, only the Julian→Gregorian day shift applies.

The `convert_calendar` tool isn't available in this environment, but the skill's documentation covers this exact example. Here is a clear, step-by-step explanation:

---

## What "25 March 1750/1" Means

This is called **double-dating** — a scribal convention used in England before the calendar reform of September 1752.

### The Problem It Solves

Before 1752, England's **legal year began on 25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January. That means the same date could carry two different year numbers depending on which system you were using:

| System | Year start | What it calls this date |
|---|---|---|
| **Old Style (OS)** — England's legal calendar | 25 March | 1750 |
| **New Style (NS)** — modern/Gregorian reckoning | 1 January | 1751 |

March 25 is the **exact boundary** — the last day of OS year 1750 shading into the first day of OS year 1751. Scribes resolved the ambiguity by writing **both years**: `1750/1`.

### Conversion

| | Value |
|---|---|
| **Record states** | 25 March 1750/1 |
| **Rule applied** | Double-dated year → use the later (New Style) year |
| **Modern date** | **25 March 1751** |

---

## Which Year to Use in Your Research Notes

**Use 1751** as your working date — that is the New Style year and the one historians and genealogical standards expect.

**Best practice:** preserve the record's original notation alongside it, so your source is transparent:

> *Marriage: 25 March 1751 (recorded as "25 March 1750/1," Old Style)*

This way anyone reading your notes can see exactly what the register said and how you interpreted it. Do **not** silently record it as 1750 — that would place the event in the wrong year by modern reckoning.

---

### One More Thing to Check

The double-date resolves only the **year**. Since this marriage predates Britain's 1752 adoption of the Gregorian calendar, the **day** is still in the Julian calendar — 11 days behind the Gregorian equivalent. Whether you need to convert the day depends on your purpose:

- **Genealogical research notes** → keep the Julian day as recorded (25 March 1751 OS). That is standard practice.
- **Correlating with a Gregorian event in another country** → add 11 days: 5 April 1751 Gregorian.

For most family history work, the Julian day is correct to keep as-is; just note the year as **1751**.

The `convert_calendar` tool is not available in this environment, but the skill's own regime table covers this case exactly — and it's a fascinating one. Here's the full answer:

---

## 30 February 1712, Stockholm — Not an OCR Error

**This is a genuine calendar date.** February 30, 1712 was a real day in Sweden, and it is one of the most unusual dates in European calendar history.

---

### What happened

Sweden attempted a *gradual* transition from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar, starting in 1700 by skipping leap days one at a time. They correctly skipped the 1700 leap day — but then failed to skip the leap days in **1704 and 1708**. By 1712, Sweden's "Swedish calendar" was only **1 day ahead of Julian** instead of the planned 10, leaving it on an idiosyncratic system used nowhere else in the world.

To fix the mess and revert cleanly to the Julian calendar, Sweden added **two** leap days in February 1712 — both February 29 **and February 30**. That extra day brought them back into sync with the Julian calendar. Sweden didn't finally adopt the Gregorian calendar until **1753**.

---

### The conversion

| Calendar | Date |
|---|---|
| **Swedish calendar (original record)** | **30 February 1712** |
| Julian (Old Style) | 29 February 1712 |
| Gregorian (New Style) | **11 March 1712** |

*Rule applied: Swedish 30 Feb 1712 = Julian 29 Feb 1712; then +11 days (1700–1799 offset) = Gregorian 11 Mar 1712.*

---

### What to record

- **Transcribe the record as written:** `30 February 1712` (Swedish calendar) — never silently alter a source date.
- **Note the calendar system** when citing it: "30 Feb 1712 (Swedish calendar)."
- **For cross-referencing** with records from other jurisdictions, use the Gregorian equivalent: **11 March 1712**.

This date is a reliable hallmark that the scribe was working in the Swedish calendar — which actually lends it a degree of authenticity rather than undermining it.
